title: Ines and the House
premise: Hazel Winterbourne, a pest controller with a habit of counting doors and keeping meticulous logs, is called to a remote house where the 'infestation' leaves fingerprints on the inside of sealed windows. Setting up sleep recorders to monitor the family, Hazel captures something impossible: a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud, in the voice of the missing daughter, Ines. As night falls and the exits begin to miscount themselves, Hazel learns the family invited something in years ago to survive a tragedy — and it has been wearing Ines ever since. To leave alive, Hazel must decide whether justice for Ines means destroying the house and everyone bound to it, or letting the thing walk out at sunrise in a stolen body.
about_author: G. M. Pemberton is the pen name of a former building surveyor who spent a decade inspecting derelict properties across northern England, where they developed an abiding unease about houses that feel occupied when they are empty. They write horror that treats architecture as memory and infestations as unfinished business.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Hazel Winterbourne, POV. A routine pest-control callout to Wintermoor House: scratching in the walls, but the client insists it's not rats. Hazel notices the front door count is wrong — five doors outside, six inside. The emotional beat is professional skepticism curdling into unease as the house's geometry quietly refuses to add up.

chapters.title: Fingerprints on Glass
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Sealed from the outside, every window bears small fingerprints pressed against the interior glass — dusted, deliberate, arranged like a signature. The mother, Corinne Vale, watches Hazel too calmly. Beat: dread deepens as Hazel realizes someone wants to be found, or wants Hazel to find them.

chapters.title: The Vales
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Meet the household: Corinne, her withdrawn son Tobias, and the absent daughter Ines, who 'stays in her room.' Her door is padlocked from the outside. Corinne's hospitality is aggressive, almost ritualistic — tea Hazel must drink, rooms Hazel must not enter. Beat: the sense of being managed, of rules serving something other than safety.

chapters.title: Bait Stations
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Hazel sets traps and monitoring equipment, including sleep recorders in the hallways, and finds gnawed wood that isn't wood — fibrous, warm, faintly pulsing. That night, from a motel, Hazel reviews the first recordings. Beat: professional routine as armor, already cracking.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. The recording captures Corinne asleep, murmuring questions — and a second voice answering in a child's register, patient and precise. It knows things about Hazel's own past. Beat: vertigo; the case stops being vermin and becomes testimony.

chapters.title: Ines
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Returning by daylight, Hazel meets Ines properly — a girl of perhaps twelve who doesn't blink enough and asks Hazel's childhood nickname, which no living person knows. She says, 'They keep me because I'm useful.' Beat: pity and terror braided together; Hazel begins to believe.

chapters.title: House Rules
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Corinne lays out explicit rules: never answer if spoken to after midnight, never open the sixth door, always let Ines eat first. Tobias, breaking silence, whispers that his sister died nine years ago. Beat: the family's survival rituals exposed as a covenant, and Hazel is now inside its terms.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: Tobias, POV. Flashback chapter: nine years ago, drowning grief after a fire killed their father, Corinne performed a neighbor's rite — inviting 'whatever remains' into the house to fill the empty room. It came wearing Ines's shape. Beat: guilt as architecture; the horror was chosen, lovingly, desperately.

chapters.title: Miscount
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Hazel returns to collect equipment and finds eleven doors where there were six, corridors that loop back to the kitchen. The van won't start; the phone shows full signal and dead air. Beat: claustrophobia — the house has decided Hazel stays until sunrise, and sunrise is fourteen hours away.

chapters.title: The Recordings, Continued
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Trapped in the kitchen, Hazel plays back accumulated tapes: the entity has been interviewing Corinne nightly, extracting confessions — she locked the real Ines out during the fire and lied about it. Beat: the horror reframes as a trial; the house is a courtroom and Corinne is the accused.

chapters.title: Corinne's Defense
chapters.summary: Corinne, POV. Corinne justifies herself to the dark: she was nineteen, terrified, the smoke too thick; the thing in Ines's shape promised the family would live if she fed it truth nightly. Beat: tragic complicity — she believes she made a bargain, not a crime, and cannot stop paying installments.

chapters.title: Tobias Breaks
chapters.summary: Tobias, POV. Tobias confronts his mother with the recordings Hazel shared, screaming that he watched her lock the door. The house responds — walls breathing, the sixth door rattling. Beat: the covenant cracks under accusation; the entity grows stronger as truths surface, feeding on admitted guilt.

chapters.title: The Sixth Door
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Following the sound of scratching, Hazel opens the forbidden door and finds the real Ines's room preserved since the fire — a burned bed, a melted music box, and hundreds of tally marks scratched inside the closet. Beat: grief as evidence; the girl was never invited out.

chapters.title: Negotiation
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Hazel speaks directly to the entity through the recorder: what does it want? Its answer, in layered voices: a verdict. Nine years of nightly confession and it still isn't satisfied — it wants Corinne to say the sentence aloud, and no one has ever asked it what happens after. Beat: Hazel shifts from victim to advocate, bargaining with something that may be a ghost or a god.

chapters.title: The Neighbor's Rite
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Searching the cellar, Hazel finds the original rite's instructions — written by a woman named Ada Merrick, who ran this covenant for three families before the Vales. The final page warns: the invited one leaves at sunrise wearing whoever confessed most completely. Beat: the trap's true teeth revealed; survival has a body price.

chapters.title: Confession Most Complete
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, interwoven. Each member of the house confesses privately to the dark — Tobias his resentments, Corinne her lie, even Hazel a buried failure from a previous callout where someone died. The walls grow warm; doors multiply. Beat: escalating dread as honesty becomes currency and everyone spends it.

chapters.title: Sunrise Terms
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. With two hours to dawn, Hazel proposes a counter-rite from Merrick's notes: name the guilty freely, release the innocent, and the entity must take only what it came for. The entity agrees — but insists Corinne speak the sentence herself, unprompted. Beat: taut negotiation; justice outside any law, arbitrated by the injured party.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Corinne, POV. Alone before the sixth door, Corinne finally says it: 'I left my daughter to burn, and I have kept her corpse talking ever since.' The house exhales. Every false door closes at once. Beat: catharsis and horror fused — the truth frees the house and damns its keeper.

chapters.title: What Walks Out
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. At sunrise the front door opens onto ordinary morning light. The entity, unmasked as the true Ines — small, burned, unbearably sad — steps past Hazel, pauses, and says thank you. Then it walks into the light and comes apart like ash off a log. Beat: devastating tenderness; the monster was the mourner all along.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Corinne, hollowed and free, surrenders to police for Ines's death; Tobias goes to an aunt. Hazel files the strangest invoice of their career and deletes the recordings — then keeps one. Beat: exhausted reckoning; survival achieved, but at the cost of everything the family built to avoid the truth.

chapters.title: The Kept Recording
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Weeks later, unable to resist, Hazel plays the saved file. Ines's voice answers a question Hazel never asked aloud: 'You'll be called again. Some houses keep more than one.' Beat: quiet, lingering dread — Hazel's empathy has made them a door.

chapters.title: Count Your Doors
chapters.summary: Hazel, POV. Final chapter: a new callout arrives — a flat across town, scratching in the walls, fingerprints on sealed glass. Hazel counts the doors twice before entering, pockets the recorder, and steps inside anyway. Beat: resolved yet haunted closure; the price of survival is that you keep surviving into the next dark house.
